5298: Oceanic whitetip sharks (Carcharhinus longimanus) were listed as threatened under the Endangered Species Act in 2018, and stock assessments indicate that populations in the western and central Pacific are historically and currently overfished. However, large data gaps remain in relation to the basic biology, ecology and population structure of this species. Photographic identification is a common and non-invasive method used to evaluate metrics of elasmobranch population demographics, abundance, residency and movement, and social behaviors. The main Hawaiian Islands are a known ‘hotspot’ for C. longimanus where they typically exhibit seasonal residency; a finding that is also supported by local fisher knowledge. This study describes the results of the Hawaii Community Tagging Program, a citizen science initiative in which fishers, divers and snorkelers submitted images of C. longimanus interactions around the main Hawaiian Islands beginning in 2008. Over 2000 images of C. longimanus were analyzed, and dorsal fin patterns were used to determine the number of unique and resighted individuals. To date, this study has identified 313 unique individuals with 15 resights; the sex ratio of females to males is approximately 2:1 (169 females and 81 males identified). We identified 45 females (~26%) with scarring or injuries from potential mating interactions and 85 individuals (~34%) carried evidence of previous fishing interactions. The information obtained from this study can help provide baseline information regarding the population demographics, residency and fishery interactions of C. longimanus around the main Hawaiian islands to help inform conservation and management measures for this protected species.

5299: Whale sharks are globally threatened; in Peru, there is no further regulation for the species than a fishing ban. Since 2014, we have been working in northern Peru with local communities to create awareness and gather data of whale shark encounters. In 2018, we start training stakeholders, such as fishermen and tour operators in how to offer responsible whale shark tourism activities to help them improve their practice and to help us collect data for the project. We implemented workshops to present the Best Practice Guidelines, and to receive feedback. We used an ethogram to collect whale shark behavior related to the boat and swimmers during fieldwork, additionally in every encounter we recorded injuries if found. To date, we have trained 53 boat Capitan and crew, in data collection and we have recommended the best practices for observation and swimming with the species. During fieldwork, we found that 85% of the sharks react to the swimmers by changing direction (89%), diving (61%), and/or swimming faster (59%). Moreover, 88% of sharks were encountered with injuries or signs of being injured recently. The recommendations from the training workshops were collected, and together with our results, a manual for good practices for whale shark tourism was prepared for the Peruvian government which is now in its final stage of review.
5300: Elasmobranchs (sharks and rays) face a range of conservation challenges contributing to extensive population declines. Consequently, there has been considerable global effort to address these declines and the IUCN’s Shark Specialist Group (SSG) has been central to many of these efforts by bringing together experts from around the world. For the first time, an Aquarium Working Group (AWG) has been formed within the SSG to recognize the role which public aquaria play in the conservation of sharks and rays. The AWG has nine members from around the world, and has identified four priority tasks: 1. Develop a position statement for the SSG on the role of aquariums in elasmobranch conservation. 2. Compile life history information from Critically Endangered elasmobranchs in aquariums to inform conservation action, with a focus on sawfishes, rhino rays (wedgefishes and guitarfishes), and south American freshwater stingrays. 3. Develop a SSG position statement on ex-situ elasmobranch release, rescue, and re-introduction. 4. Develop SSG messaging and graphics on elasmobranch conservation for aquarium exhibits, outreach, and education programs. In addition to introducing the AWG, we will present the findings of a global survey focused on the current extent of elasmobranch release, rescue, and re-introduction within the aquarium community.
5301: Tagging programs are key to evaluate post-release mortality of Endangered, Threatened, and Protected species that are caught incidentally in fishing operations. This work presents results of a tagging program conducted on purse seiners under ECHEBASTAR company, aimed at assessing post-release survival of silky sharks caught in association with tuna schools and released according to the Code of Good Practices. During two fishing trips sixty silky sharks were tagged (28 and 32 silky sharks in the first and second trip, respectively) with 37 SPATs and 23 MiniPATs, and blood samples were collected in 124 sharks for lactate concentration measurement to be used as an indicator of shark survival. A vitality index based on state and behavior at release was also assigned to all the sharks caught accidentally. The overall predicted survival of silky shark was close to 40% based on vitality index derived from tagged sharks. The overall survival rate predicted using lactate concentration threshold was more variable among trips going from 35% to 60% in the first and second trip, respectively. Shark survivorship decreased as the fishing operation advanced and vitality index declined. This post-release survival estimates duplicate previous estimations on purse seiners. The experience gained over time in the application of best practices and fauna release devices (i.e. the bycatch conveyor belt) installed on-board contributed to reducing shark mortality in the purse seiner fishery.
5302: Mesh net fisheries can result in bycatch of species of conservation interest (SOCI) such as dugongs and hammerhead sharks. In the Great Barrier Reef, bycatch mortality of both SOCI and of undersized/unwanted fishes has severely affected the fishery's social license and has exacerbated conflict, especially with recreational fishers. However, trap type gears can help reduce mortality. Tunnel nets are large mobile fish traps that guide the catch into a tunnel where the catch remains free-swimming until brailling and sorting. Bycatch is released in very good condition. Larger species including SOCI such as marine turtles, sharks, and rays are prevented from entering the tunnel by large mesh grids, and remain free swimming in a holding area until release. Increasing regulatory pressure and public scrutiny of net fisheries in the Great Barrier Reef are driving efforts to find solutions to improve sustainability and community support for fisheries while maintaining fisher livelihoods. Here we describe the results of a small-scale feasibility trial using tunnel net gears in the shallow coastal waters of the Great Barrier Reef. Expert tunnel net fishers worked with local net fishers to trial and test the use of tunnel nets. The gear works, fishers can catch fish and SOCI species such as hammerheads and batoids were released unharmed. However, the suitability and feasibility of these gears requires careful consideration and while the gear is technically feasible, its commercial viability remains unknown. The perspectives and attitudes of commercial fishers and other stakeholders engaged during the trials will also be presented.
5303: Munk’s pygmy devil ray (Mobula munkiana) are medium size, zooplanktivorous filter feeding elasmobranchs. Native to the Eastern Tropical Pacific and listed as Vulnerable on the IUCN Red List, their aggregative behavior exacerbates its captured as targeted catch and as incidental bycatch in both artisanal and large-scale fisheries. By employing multiple approaches (acoustic telemetry, stable isotopes, traditional tagging, and photometry), we collected data to complete life history gaps such as the identification of critical habitats, migratory routes, and aggregative behavior patterns at the Mexican Pacific. At the same time, we assess their rates of post-release mortality from artisanal gillnet fisheries in Mexico using acoustic tags to understand the population-level effects of survival due to fisheries impacts on this species. To date, results of acoustic tags in M. munkiana individuals (n=108), traditional tags (n=95), blood samples for isotopes analysis (n=69) and photometry surveys (n=60) have allow us to describe a nursery area within the Marine Protected Area of Espiritu Santo Archipelago, and a reproductive ground for the species in La Ventana Bay in Baja California Sur. Pupping and mating periods are linked to spring and summer (April to June) seasons. Size and sex segregation is present in this species, including a differentiation in their diet as they grow, switching from euphausiids to mysids as main prey. Migratory patterns repeat across four years connecting at least 2 different Marine Protected Areas in the southern Gulf of California.

5304: The sandbar shark (Carcharhinus plumbeus) has a global distribution and is caught by commercial and recreational fishers. We assessed the post-release survival of sandbar sharks caught in longline surveys conducted in Western Australia (WA) using an integrated approach that combined the use of hook-timers, release condition staging, satellite tagging, and blood physiology (adrenocorticotropic hormone, corticosterone, and lactate). Of the 57 individuals examined, 88% were “alive and strong” with 100% initial survival when released after a maximum of four hours on the hook. Of the 13 satellite-tagged individuals, 100% survived. Sharks dived up to 307 m deep and showed cyclical depth movement patterns with some individuals moving up and down the water column both day and night, while others moved almost exclusively at night, corresponding with the movement patterns of squid, a common prey item of sandbar sharks. The concentration of blood metabolites did not show a linear pattern with time on hook. The 100% survival rate within four hours on the hooks suggests the use of longlines for surveying sandbar shark abundance has no deleterious consequences.

5305: Fisheries bycatch is a significant threat to shark populations worldwide. Thus, understanding bycatch fates – if an animal is retained or discarded, dear or alive – is key information for estimating the bycatch impact on shark populations. Here, we analyze the data on fates of sharks caught in the Convention Area of three tuna Regional Fisheries Management Organizations (RFMO): Western Pacific (WCPFC), Indian (IOTC) and Atlantic (ICCAT) Oceans, to infer bycatch fate patterns between 2012 and 2018. We calculate fate proportions from each RFMO for 68 taxa identified at the genus or species level. We find substantial variation in the reported categories and post-capture fates across RFMOs. No sharks were reported retained in WCPFC, with sharks being either discarded alive (average 66%) or dead (average 33%). While live discards were the most frequent in IOTC, they report 15% retention on average. Live discards show an increasing trend in ICCAT over the same period, peaking at 25% in 2017. Given the different rates of observer coverage for each RFMO, we refrain from comparing bycatch fates across them. Regarding CITES-listed species, we observed 100% live discards of whale sharks in ICCAT and IOTC, while almost 100% retention of mako sharks caught by ICCAT managed vessels. Mako sharks were also the most frequently retained species in IOTC. Overall, our analysis demonstrates that ICCAT represents most shark retention across RFMOs, which primarily comprises mako sharks. We further note that our results are likely influenced by the scarcity of available observer data, especially in IOTC and ICCAT.

5306: The bronze whaler or copper shark (Carcharhinus brachyurus) is a large coastal shark with a wide distribution across a highly heterogeneous environment and is one of the most exploited elasmobranchs in South Africa. Here the aim was to assess the distribution of neutral and adaptive genomic diversity in this vulnerable species in the South-East Atlantic and South-West Indian Ocean region using putatively neutral and candidate single nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs). Samples were collected across a representative distribution range from the east coast of South Africa to Angola and prepared for massively parallel sequencing on an Illumina platform using a restriction site-associated DNA (3RAD) library preparation protocol. Generated sequencing reads were processed with an optimized bioinformatic pipeline and resulted in thousands of SNPs genotyped in 64 samples. The analyses of putatively neutral SNPs revealed moderate and evenly distributed levels of genomic diversity across sampling sites. Multivariate and clustering analyses demonstrated a high degree of gene flow with no significant population structuring among or within ocean basins. Genotype-environment analysis performed using redundancy analysis identified SNPs significantly associated with mean sea surface temperature, pH and oxygen. These candidate SNPs indicated the presence of at least two clusters and deep divergence between individuals from South Africa, Namibia and Angola. These results provide evidence for local adaptation to specific environmental conditions in a highly mobile shark despite high levels of gene flow. This is expected to inform management strategies and policy at the national and regional level for conservation of C. brachyurus populations.

5307: Nigeria is one of the shark fishing nations in Africa, but its catch data on elasmobranchs are still recorded in aggregates ‘sharks’ and ‘rays’ with no further species-specific details. The major reason for this is most of the shark specimens look identical in morphology and field identification of some closely related species is difficult. Also, fisheries managers and scientists find it tricky to identify poorly preserved and deteriorating specimens or those lacking the key diagnostic features for identification. This study used DNA barcoding as a method to identify shark species from four different landing areas off the Nigerian Coast and two major fish markets in Lagos, Nigeria. 128 dorsal fins were sampled. 27 of these did not provide successful sequence results, while 101 (77.7%) provided a Chondrichthyan sequence that was matched to reference specimens in a DNA barcode database. Three species of sharks were identified, with all three of CITES importance, (17.8% Critically Endangered, 61.4% Endangered, 20.8% Vulnerable). Fisheries managers can use this information to assist in identification and make informed decisions on conservation and management issues.

5308:
All living organisms leave traces of DNA in their environments. This DNA can be released through urine, gametes, blood, mucus, skin loss etc. This DNA can be collected in the water column through filtration, and is then called environmental DNA or eDNA. The metabarcoding of this eDNA is a new technicque which can then be used to accurately estimate marine biodiversity with more accurate value, including rare, cryptic, elusive or invasive species.

The aim of this project is to obtain genetic sequences from sharks, skates, rays and marine mammals at a global scale with a view to assign species to their 12S mitochondrion barcodes from eDNA samples. The barcode database is the cornerstone of any eDNA study in conservation. Thus, we’re looking for collaborations with aquariums and museums worldwide to collect tissues (fin clip (1.5 x 0.5 cm) on the caudal fin or blood (200μL) store in pure alcohol or frozen for missing species. With this sample (at least two individuals from each species) we will be able to extract the DNA and then complete the 12S marker gene database for these species. The advantage with this technique in addition to revealing the dark diversity is to be non-invasive for the species. Ultimately it will improve the knowledge (biogeography, presence in marine reserves, depth) such a collaboration would make it possible to take advantage of the competences of each one for a common objective: the conservation of threatened species.
5309: Due to their exceptional levels of functional genetic diversity, genes of the major histocompatibility complex (MHC) represent ideal candidates to reveal genetic differentiation among geographical regions and ultimately improving genetic stock identification of commercially exploited shark species. In addition, from an evolutionary perspective, because of the major role of MHC in pathogen resistance, MHC diversity can be expected to be locally adapted to pathogens, resulting in a more pronounced genetic structure in these genes compared to neutral expectations. Alternatively, balancing selection at the geographic scale can lead to a weaker genetic structure compared to the neutral population structure if, for instance, prevailing pathogens are the same over the whole study area. To distinguish between these scenarios, we sequenced MHC-IIβ genes using high-throughput sequencing technology in an extensive number of small-spotted catsharks (Scyliorhinus canicula) sampled across the entire European geographic distribution (N=600). All samples were also genotyped with 11 neutral microsatellite markers as a baseline to contrast with MHC diversity and genetic structure. Our preliminary results suggest that this species has three different MHC-IIβ genes, with the typical characteristics of functional MHC-IIβ genes: high number of alleles and high sequence divergence between alleles. We also show that MHC diversity in catsharks vary across regions, probably involving both demographic and selective forces. This study provides interesting perspectives for the understanding of evolutionary mechanisms involved in MHC diversity but also shows that the MHC system provides prime markers to stock delimitation, which is essential knowledge for sustainable long-term management of vulnerable marine species.

5310: The small-spotted catshark Scyliorhinus canicula, is a demersal Scyliorhinid shark species commonly found in Mediterranean and Northeastern Atlantic waters. The philopatric and sedentary nature of female S. canicula, along with its high abundance among bottom trawl bycatch; stock exploitation resilience and widespread distribution could support the xenobiotic biomonitoring potential of this species. A year long study was performed from November 2019 to November 2020 within which 300 mature female specimens were gathered. Intramuscular Cu, Pb and Cd concentrations were determined via graphite furnace atomic absorption spectroscopy (GFAAS), while the digestive tract of each captured individual was pre-treated via alkaline extraction and vacuum filtration for its subsequent visual characterisation and polymer species Identification via RAMAN spectroscopy. Stable mean concentrations of Pb, Cd and Cu were observed in muscle tissues throughout the year with significant differences occurring only between non consecutive months. Spatial analysis shows the existence of well-defined heavy metal concentration hotspots occurring in certain points of the study site within which certain individuals surpassed the 0.05 and 0.3 µg·g-1 (ww) maximum threshold for safe human consumption stablished by the European commission Regulation (EC) No 1881/2006). Macroplastics, mesoplastic and microplastics were identified within Scyliorhinus canicula gastric tracts with plastic counts ranging between 3 to 32 units. Different plastic polymers were identified, with a higher presence of Polyethylene terephthalate (PET), Polyamide (PA) and polypropylene (PP).
5311: Global climate change has fundamental impacts on the structure and function of marine environments. Examining the associated effects on threatened species using these environments is a major challenge for scientists and conservationists. This study investigated the effects of the 2016 extreme temperature event on the apparent survival and body condition of juvenile populations of two threatened carcharhinid shark species using a nursery habitat at St Joseph atoll, Seychelles. 228 blacktip reef sharks Carcharhinus melanopterus and 189 sicklefin lemon sharks Negaprion acutidens were caught during mark-recapture experiments over four years from 2014-2017. Mark-recapture modelling was used to estimate apparent survival (φ) and probability of recapture (p) for both species. Best-fit models indicated distinct differences around the 2016 thermal event with a 12% reduction in apparent survival of C. melanopterus (φ - 2014 + 15 = 0.65, φ - 2016+2017 = 0.53) and a 14% reduction in N. acutidens (φ – 2014, 15, 17 = 0.82, φ - 2016 = 0.68). Fulton’s condition factor was used estimate changes in body condition over the study period and evidenced significant decreases in body condition around the thermal event for both species. Findings from this study indicate a significant effect of large-scale ocean warming events on the fitness and survival of juvenile shark populations. How to tackle this ubiquitous threat will be a key question for shark science moving forward.

5312:
Plastic is ubiquitous in the environment and is known to have negative impacts on marine ecosystems. Marine organisms can entangle in discarded fishing gear, ingest plastic debris, and accumulate leached toxic chemicals in their tissues. Filter-feeding megafaunal elasmobranchs, including the reef manta ray (Mobula alfredi), giant manta ray (Mobula birostris), whale shark (Rhincodon typus) and basking shark (Cetorhinus maximus) are exposed to the risk of plastic pollution, due to their low trophic level and their habitat overlap with known areas of plastic accumulation. They are also important flagship species for conservation with an additional value for ecotourism.

This piece of work explores the global geographical overlap between these species and plastic distribution to identify the populations at risk. We use publicly available databases of species occurrences to build a maximum entropy distribution model for the four species. We then overlay those with plastic debris data, including macroplastics such as discarded fishing gear, and microplastics distributions from existing plastic dispersal model outputs. This allows us to calculate the exposure of the four species to the risks of plastic ingestion and entanglement in discarded fishing gear.

This overlap analysis will allow us to build testable predictions of ingestion and entanglement risk based on overlap between debris and filter-feeder distributions, and in the future assess these predictions by evaluating existing evidence of exposure at different locations. We also hope the results of this study will focus mitigation policies and actions to the relevant priority locations.
5313: Sound in the marine environment is used across taxa to inform behaviour, however human activities now often pollute natural cuescapes, masking or modifying important information. Anthropogenic disruption of marine sensory landscapes is known to negatively affect the distribution, behaviour and physiology of marine mammals, teleost fish and various invertebrate phyla. While relatively little is known about the mechanisms and capabilities of hearing in sharks, multiple studies have shown that they detect and respond (physiologically and behaviourally) to low frequency sounds (<1500 Hz). During juvenile development, sharks often display site fidelity to coastal habitats, such as mangroves, coral reefs and seagrass beds, where human disturbance can often be concentrated. One extreme example of this is in the Biscayne Bay, Miami, USA, where there is a high density and diversity of sharks along a heavily developed coastline with high levels of boating activity. Understanding which sounds sharks detect, respond to and are influenced by in situ has received little attention. To address this knowledge gap, we present the characterisation of the Biscayne Bay soundscape from an elasmobranch perspective (i.e. mapping spatial and temporal patterns of acoustic conditions at low frequencies, including in the particle motion domain). Specific attention is paid to describing the biological and anthropogenic contributions to the soundscape that fall within known hearing sensitivities. Our results are discussed in the context of potential ecological roles of sound in shark ecology and the impacts of anthropogenic noise on sharks. We will use this opportunity to open conversations on how deepening our understanding of elasmobranch sensory systems and multi-sensory integration may be applied to conservation initiatives.
5314: Plastics are synthetic materials made by long-life polymers, that persist for hundreds of years in the environment. This is the real plastic pollution problem. Every year enormous amounts of plastic debris are poured in the marine environment. In this work we investigated the presence of plastic remains in the stomach contents of three populations of Scyliorhinus canicula and Galeus melastomus, two of the most common deep demersal shark species in Mediterranean, along the Tyrrhenian coast of Italy. Both shark species have an opportunistic benthic scavenger behaviour. We obtained animals thanks to MEDITS survey and stomach contents were analysed in laboratory under a microscope. We discriminated plastic by shape (fibres, scrapes, sphere, and film) and colour (orange, black, white, blue, yellow, red, grey and green). The most common plastic remains founded in stomach were scrapes in both sharks’ populations in Lazio, film for lesser spotted dogfish and fibres for blackmouth catshark in Tuscany, and fibers for Scyliorhinus canicula and films for Galeus melastomus in Liguria. About colour discrimination, Scyliorhinus canicula ingested more grey and yellow plastics in the three populations than Galeus melastomus, which ingested, on the contrary, more black and white fragments. Ingestion seemed to be accidental for shapes, but for colours maybe the feeding behaviour of the two species could affect the choice.
5315: Many of the world’s shark populations are in decline indicating the need for improved conservation and management. A better understanding of their distribution and habitat requirements is vital for habitat protection and effective fisheries management, essential to maintain viable populations. Alongside this, oceans are warming worldwide and how such temperature variation will influence sharks requires investigation. We used statistical modelling tools to assess occurrence, habitat suitability and potential climate change effects for pelagic sharks from the Carcharhinidae and Lamnidae families in Australian waters and the adjacent high seas using shark occurrence records compiled from offshore commercial fisheries. We collated environmental and spatial predictors known to affect shark occurrence and developed generalised linear models to determine the extent of suitable habitat for pelagic sharks within the Australian continental Exclusive Economic Zone (EEZ). As well managed and appropriately located marine protected areas (MPAs) may enhance shark conservation, we quantified the amount of suitable habitat contained within existing MPAs. Our results indicate sea surface temperature (SST) to be a significant predictor of pelagic shark distribution, and even though highly suitable habitat was limited in MPA zones closed to fishing, Australia has strict fisheries legislation protecting pelagic sharks. With SST an important determinant of pelagic shark habitat suitability, we then examined the impact of increasing ocean temperatures in the future using an ensemble of climate models under two emission scenarios. Our predictions highlight how future SSTs are likely to shift the location of suitable pelagic shark habitat for both shark families within the Australian EEZ.

5316: Concerning pollution, non-essential metals have been historically present in the Mediterranean, sometimes reaching levels that could be harmful for marine biota. Despite the fact that batoids are a significant part of Mediterranean food webs, little is known about the threats that this metal pollution may represent to this group. In this study, we analyzed mercury (Hg), lead (Pb) and cadmium (Cd), in livers and muscle from 90 batoids of three different species: Dasyatis pastinaca (N=30), Myliobatis aquila (N=30) and, Torpedo torpedo (N=30). Our aim was to quantify these metals in a historically polluted area, the coast next to l’Albufera (East Spain), a coastal lagoon that discharges water into the sea. Besides, we studied whether metal concentration could be correlated with the different position in the food web of these species and with their size. In general, mercury was the most abundant metal, closely followed by lead and, lastly, cadmium was found in very low concentrations (mean±SD w.w. in muscle: 31.4±11.2 µg/g of Hg; 16.51±4.8 µg/g of Pb and 0.33±0.2 µg/g of Cd; in liver: 31.4±11.2 µg/g of Hg; 16.51±4.8 µg/g of Pb and 0.33±0.2 µg/g of Cd). Regarding biometric parameters, D. pastinaca and T. torpedo showed the highest metal concentration; in accordance to their higher position in the foodweb, in comparison with M. aquila. Results indicate that these batoids do not seem to be threatened by metals in the area, possibly reflecting either a low metallic pollution of their surroundings or their low mobilization from the sediments.
5317: Continental shelf and deep ocean waters are subjected to anthropogenic pressures such as fishing and climate change-related environmental stressors. Sharks s in temperate waters are predicted to move poleward in response to climate change. However, their distribution through space and time remains poorly understood, limiting the potential to understand how they are responding to environmental stressors. Knowledge of the abundance and its environmental drivers of this threatened marine group is needed to inform sustainable management. Generalized additive models and mapping were performed on a 26-year scientific survey time-series in the Norwegian Sea and environmental data to model the impact of climate change on the distribution and abundance of two shark species living in deep and cold waters: Etmopterus spinax, and Galeus melastomus, at the northern fringe of their ranges, together with the distribution of their potential prey species. Both shark species significantly shifted their abundance northwards, and local abundances have declined to various degrees over the last seven years. The warming of northern waters across the last three decades seems the main driver of a northward shift in the local abundance of these two shark species and their prey. This indicates that climate change is likely a major driver of large-scale abundance patterns for sharks, even among deep-sea species. In a global warming context, survey data, long-term series and international cooperation are required to record extended shifts and better conserve transboundary species.
5318: The Bull Shark, Carcharhinus leucas, faces varying levels of exploitation in fisheries and shark control programs around the world. Baseline information regarding the species’ life-history, reproductive behaviour and global or regional connectivity is crucial to evaluate fishery impacts and its conservation status. In this study, we obtained samples from nearly 1,000 sharks from 19 different sampling locations for the first global-scale assessment of population structure in this cosmopolitan species. Using a recently developed DNA capture approach (DArTcap), all samples were genotyped for 3,400 nuclear markers. In addition, the full mitochondrial genomes of 384 Indo-Pacific samples were also sequenced. Reproductive isolation was inferred at an ocean basin scale (eastern Pacific, western Atlantic, eastern Atlantic, Indo-West Pacific) with signals of separate island populations (Japan and Fiji). Bull Sharks appear to maintain reproductive connectivity using shallow coastal waters as dispersal corridors, whereas large oceanic distances and historical land bridges act as barriers. The removal of Bull Sharks from insular populations, such as Japan and Fiji, may precipitate local decline that cannot readily be replenished by immigration, which can in turn affect ecosystem dynamics. We note that females tend to return to the same area for reproduction, which makes them more vulnerable to local threats and an important focus for management actions. Finally, we provide new genetic markers that can assign provenance and sex from DNA samples which will prove valuable for future monitoring of the international fin and meat trade.

5319: Oceanic (Mobula birostris) and reef manta rays (Mobula alfredi) are among the most iconic species in our oceans yet significant knowledge gaps remain about fundamental aspects of their biology. For example, it remains a mystery both how their widespread distributions have arisen and the extent to which populations are connected within them. This information is crucial not only for establishing appropriate spatial scales for management, but for assessing population viability into the future. We address this using high-resolution genomic data for over 200 manta ray samples (M. birostris: n = 120, M. alfredi: n = 126) collected from across their entire distribution. We show that despite their recent divergence, oceanic and reef mantas display striking differences in population structure at a global scale, which is associated with significantly different levels of genetic diversity both between and within species. These findings indicate fundamental differences in colonisation strategy and migratory behaviour and highlight potentially vulnerable populations in need of heightened protection. We will examine these results in light of what is currently known about manta rays and discuss our findings in the context of global conservation management.

5320: Blacktip reef sharks (Carcharhinus melanopterus) are a widespread Indo-Pacific reef shark species listed as vulnerable on the IUCN Red List for endangered species because of poaching, habitat loss and anthropogenic perturbations. Around the Island of Moorea (French Polynesia), the Center for Island Research and Environmental Observatory (CRIOBE) sampled 1700 adult and juvenile blacktip reef shark fin clips over a 13-year timespan. In Moorea, blacktip reef sharks give birth in shallow coastal lagoon areas, enabling neonate and juvenile sharks to withstand predation and to find sufficient foraging resources. For this PhD project, parentage analysis was conducted on the 1700 fin clip samples using genetic analyses (microsatellite DNA markers) to reconstruct the pedigree of the population. The resulting genealogy aims at defining life history traits such as the number of juveniles per litter, mother offspring resource allocation at birth (by using body condition and blood metabolite data), longevity and juvenile survival rates. The pedigree will also enable to evaluate the recruitment success of adult individuals (when offspring of an adult individual reaches adulthood), natal philopatry (females returning to their birthplace to parturition) in adult female individuals and the presence of dominant individuals (individuals which, on average, have higher reproduction rates) within the population. The results will provide a better understanding of the functioning of blacktip reef shark populations making it possible to provide information to local decision makers on the best strategies that can be developed to improve reef shark conservation.

5321: Despite blue sharks (Prionace glauca) being the most prevalent and most fished of any shark species, our understanding of their population genetic structure is limited. Large-scale genetic sampling is an important tool for the conservation and management of vulnerable and elusive species and can provide greater insight into estimates of population structure, abundance, and even behavioural ecology. While traditional genetics studies have relied more heavily on invasive techniques and expertise, novel non-invasive genetic sampling can offer an effective substitute. Furthermore, less invasive techniques have the potential to increase genetic studies’ applications whilst reducing costs. This study determined the efficacy and application of using a novel non-invasive technique to collect genetic material from free-swimming blue sharks for population genetic studies. The study took place in the Celtic Sea, UK, where we collected 39 epidermal swabs from a total of 11 free-swimming blue sharks using a toothbrush and freediving approach. Regions of the mitochondrial CO1 and control region, and nuclear ribosomal ITS2 regions, were successfully amplified from the samples. Results across all three markers support the existence of low genetic variation between regions, however, genetic structuring remains a possibility that requires further investigation. Results from the mitochondrial control region showed the correct identification of individuals across multiple samples, demonstrating this method’s application for long-term mark-recapture studies. We recommend future studies investigate contamination mitigation, improvement of amplification techniques, and determine the application of samples for other population genomics analyses, such as high throughput sequencing.

5322: Thornback Ray (Raja clavata) is a relatively abundant commercial skate species occurring in coastal waters of the North-East Atlantic and Mediterranean, listed by the IUCN as Near Threatened. It is the dominant skate species caught in commercial fisheries in northern European seas. Historically, regional population declines have been observed, although increased landings indicate increases in population size in several areas over recent decades. This study describes the genetic diversity and population structure of Raja clavata hierarchically among ecoregions, spanning the Greater North Sea (GNS), Celtic Sea (CS), and Bay of Biscay and Iberian coast (BB), as well as within ecoregions by ICES Divisions. Over 8000 samples were collected (2004 – 2022) and genotyped. Subsequent quality control resulted in a SNP dataset of >4000 SNPs for analyses. Estimates of genetic diversity are provided among and within ecoregions. Small yet significant genetic differentiation was evident globally (Fst,global = 0.0042) and among all ecoregions via pairwise Fst (Fst,GNS-CS = 0.003, Fst,CS-BB = 0.007, Fst,GNS-BB = 0.009; p-values < 0.01). Only ICES Divisions 4b and 4c in the GNS (Fst,4b-4c = 0.00004, p = 0.144) showed no significant genetic differentiation within ecoregions. AMOVA, discriminant component analysis, and admixture modelling provide further evidence and describe the population structure on both hierarchical population levels investigated. This is the largest known genetic study of Raja clavata, to our knowledge. This research helps to inform stock identification and thus assessment, conservation and fisheries management, by accounting for genetic population structure at different spatial scales in the North-East Atlantic.
5323: Influence of environmental factors on prey discrimination of bait-attracted white sharks were studied over a six-year period (2008-2013) at Dyer Island Nature Reserve (Gansbaai, South Africa). This work deepens previous published study on surface predatory behaviour of bait-attracted white sharks conducted in the same area where, from 240 predator-prey interactions observed in the same period, both immature and mature white sharks were attracted from the seal shaped decoy rather than the tuna bait, except for the years 2008 and 2011. Tide ranges, underwater visibility, water temperature, and sea conditions are, in decreasing order, the factors that drive white sharks to the prey choice. High tide reduces the minimum depth from which sharks could approach seals close to the shore, while a good visibility helps the sharks to use their vision ability to implement predatory choices to energetical richer prey, the odorless seal shaped decoy. On the contrary, warmer water is associated both with an increasing and diversity of teleosts which are prey of white sharks and to an increase of phytoplankton that reduces the underwater visibility, driving them to the tuna bait choice. Finally, sea condition was almost always slightly rough, ensuring a good average underwater visibility. Recommendations for future research work at this site are presented.

5324: Many elasmobranchs exhibit complex courtship rituals. The function of large aggregations of basking sharks engaged in circling behaviour largely remains a mystery. We present, underwater and aerial video recordings of multiple circling groups of basking sharks in late summer (August to September) during years 2016–2021 in Ireland. Groups comprised females and males numbering between 6 and 23 individuals that were not filter feeding. Grouped sharks swam slowly in a clockwise or anticlockwise rotating ‘torus’ (diameter range: 17–39 m) consisting of circling individuals layered vertically from the surface to a maximum depth of 16 m. Within a torus, sharks engaged in close-following, echelon, close flank-approach or parallel swimming behaviours. Total body lengths of circling sharks overlapped known lengths of sexually mature individuals. In some toruses female body coloration was paler than that of males. Within a torus individuals associated with most other members rapidly (within minutes) indicating toroidal behaviours facilitate multiple interactions. Torus members also interacted through fin-fin and fin-body contacts, rolling to expose ventral surfaces to following sharks, and breaching behaviour. We also confirmed that a torus forms from shark following behaviour, and can change rotation direction frequently. Collectively, our observations explain a courtship function for non-feeding circling groups. This study highlights the importance of coastal waters off western Ireland as critical habitats supporting courtship reproductive behaviour of endangered basking sharks, the first such habitats identified for this species globally. This has important conservation implications for a species recently given legal protection status in Ireland.

5325: White shark movements are typically observed over large spatial scales (100s-1000s km2). However, observation of fine-scale movement behaviour of white sharks is necessary to improve our understanding of their usage of near-shore coastal areas where there is an increased probability of interactions between sharks and humans. Based on passive acoustic data from a dense, but non-triangulating, array we investigated the fine scale movement of white sharks at a coastal beach within a nursery area off Hawk’s Nest, New South Wales from 2010-2015. Using a spatial Hidden Markov Model (HMM) we were able to estimate white shark movement tracks during each shark visit to the array based on detection binning over 5-minute time intervals. The HMM also enabled direct estimation of the probability of detection as a function of distance from shark to acoustic receivers. The HMM-estimated movement tracks predict heavy utilisation of very shallow water close to the high-water mark by the sharks. Additionally, the southern end of the beach appears to be a focus for short term white shark residency at the beach. The movement tracks estimated here allowed the first high-resolution investigation of white shark movements in the Hawk’s Nest nursery area and demonstrate the potential for estimation of fine-scale position data from non-triangulating passive acoustic monitoring arrays deployed in other coastal marine areas.

5326:
Shark research and conservation efforts are typically driven by a desire to inform the status assessment and increase the level of protection afforded to the target species. However, the translation of scientific findings and or conservation initiatives into real world policy change is a persistent challenge for non-governmental organisations and academics. Basking sharks are listed by the IUCN as globally endangered. Ireland is significant to basking sharks in the Northeast Atlantic, however until 2022, they were not protected under domestic legislation. To help others overcome this disconnect we describe and review the methods that the Irish Basking Shark Group (IBSG), a volunteer research and outreach organisation, deployed to realize a change in legislative status for the species in Irish waters.

Between 2009 and 2022 the IBSG delivered approximately forty research, outreach and legislative change initiatives designed to raise the awareness, understanding and appreciation of basking sharks in Irish and International waters. No individual action or effort stream (i.e., public outreach, scientific research or political lobbying) delivered alone. Rather an integrated approach that melded internationally significant research studies with locally orientated ocean literacy initiates’ and strategically timed media campaigns provided the maximum leverage of policy makers.

Lastly, we consider how these experiences can be applied to other species or scaled up to regional forums. Our goal here is to provide a road map for similar conservation efforts through sharing our experience in attaining protection for the basking shark in Irish wildlife legislation, the first fish to be given this status.

5327: Catch-and-release fishing is an important component of ecotourism industries and scientific research worldwide, but its total impact on animal physiology, health and survival is understudied for many species of sharks. We combined biologging and blood chemistry to explore how this fisheries interaction influenced the physiology of two widely distributed, highly migratory shark species: blue sharks (Prionace glauca), and tiger sharks (Galeocerdo cuvier). Nineteen sharks were caught by drum line or rod-and-reel angling; subcutaneous body temperature measurements were taken immediately upon capture, with 6 individuals also providing subsequent subcutaneous body temperature measurements via biologging as they swam freely for several hours post-release. We found that short-term capture caused shark body temperature to increase significantly and rapidly, with increases of 0.6 – 2.7°C for blue sharks (mean 1.2 ± 0.6°C) and 0.5 – 0.9°C for tiger sharks (mean 0.7 ± 0.2°C), and with capture-induced heating rates of blue sharks averaging 0.3°C min-1 but as high as 0.8°C min-1. These heating rates were 3-8 times faster than maximum rates encountered by our biologging sharks swimming through thermally stratified waters. Biologging data showed that body temperatures underwent gradual decline after release, returning to match water temperatures approximately 10 – 40 mins post-release. Blood biochemistry showed variable lactate/glucose levels following capture; however, these concentrations weren’t correlated with the magnitude of body temperature increase, nor body size or hooking time. These perturbations of the natural state could have immediate and longer-term effects on the welfare and ecology of sharks caught and future research could focus on exploring these effects.
5329: Crustacean bottom-trawlers are responsible for 70% of discards in the south of Portugal and deep-sea sharks are expressive bycatch, due to their overlap with fishing grounds, low commercial values and/or fishing regulations. Most individuals are discarded either dead or in poor physical condition. The physiological consequences of this type of capture in elasmobranchs are poorly understood. This study analyzed stress-related physiological parameters of four common deep-sea shark, sampled from two different trawling procedures: one conducted onboard a commercial crustacean bottom-trawler (longer haul duration and heavier codend weight) and the other conducted onboard a research vessel (shorter haul duration and lighter codend weight). A total of 120 individuals from the species Etmopterus pusillus, Etmopterus spinax, Galeus melastomus and Scymnodon ringens were studied. Plasma was collected onboard and frozen until analysis. The concentrations (mmol/L) of plasma electrolytes (Na+, Cl-, Ca2+, Mg2+) and energy metabolites (glucose, lactate) were measured and related to specific trawling conditions, specimen vitality and survival. Differences between commercial and research hauls were observed. Commercial hauls were marked by significantly high concentrations of Na+, Cl-, Mg2+ and lactate, whilst research hauls presented higher concentrations of glucose and Ca2+. Specifically, commercial hauls caused significant increases in Cl- and lactate for S. ringens and Na+ for E. pusillus, and a decrease in glucose concentrations for E. pusillus. A complete analysis of the relation between physiological stress indicators and trawling variables should provide further insight to establish additional recommendations to increase the welfare and the effective management of discarded deep-sea sharks.

5330: Pelagic sharks are highly threatened by overfishing and in urgent need of science-based conservation management. A key need is improved information on the population genetic structure and diversity of these ecologically important taxa. The shortfin mako shark (Isurus oxyrinchus) is an oceanic, globally widespread species known for its capacity for long-distance movements spanning thousands of kilometers. This species is listed as globally ‘Endangered’ by the IUCN Red List of Threatened Species, and Atlantic makos are considered overfished and in decline. We investigated the population genetic dynamics of shortfin mako sharks in the Atlantic Ocean using a high-resolution, bi-organelle, multi-marker, genomics approach. We sequenced 86 complete mitochondrial genomes (mitogenomes) (16,999-17,002 bp) and genotyped 4236 single nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) in 105 sharks across the Atlantic and found contrasting patterns of genetic population structure across DNA markers. Mitogenome sequences indicated matrilineal population genetic structure across northern and southern hemispheres, while nuclear-based SNPs showed high connectivity and ocean basin-wide panmixia. Mitogenome genetic diversity in Atlantic shortfin makos was high compared to other elasmobranchs assessed at the population mitogenome level, and nuclear diversity was high compared to migratory shark species assessed with SNP markers, boding well for the genetic recovery of Atlantic shortfin makos if further population declines can be halted.

5331: Since 2007, OCEARCH has conducted 44 expeditions in nine countries focusing on comprehensive research and public awareness of sharks and other marine vertebrates. Our goal is to provide the data to return balance, abundance, and ecological health to our oceans, starting with rebuilding populations of its top predators. By donating the unique facilities, capabilities, and skilled crew of our 40m research ship to the scientific community at no cost, OCEARCH provides unprecedented access to large sharks in the wild for advanced studies of their biology, conservation status, and human impacts. Using the Google business model to build and monetize scale, we follow these principles to advance shark research: 1) broad collaboration, uniting fishermen, scientists, educators, and policymakers to rapidly increase our knowledge on sharks; 2) the 3Rs of animal research, minimizing the number of sharks needed to answer the maximum number of questions, while ensuring the health and safety of each shark studied; 3) inclusion, allowing the world to participate in real time through open access to new scientific data; and 4) innovative funding, from brand-integrated content, conscious consumerism, and philanthropy. OCEARCH has facilitated the work of more than 200 scientists in the Pacific, Atlantic, and Indian Oceans, resulting in 75 peer-reviewed publications, and we have advanced public awareness through our Global Shark TrackerTM app and website, social media, and STEM educational programs. With our multi-year study of the white shark in the Western North Atlantic completed, we are bringing our ship to Europe and the Mediterranean in 2023.

5332: With the completion of a multi-year comprehensive study of white shark biology in the Western North Atlantic (WNA) by OCEARCH and its collaborators, knowledge of the WNA population has rapidly surpassed the level previously attained in Australia and New Zealand, South Africa, and the eastern Pacific. A total of 19 expeditions along the North American Atlantic coast have supported the multidisciplinary work of 45 investigators from 30 organizations to advance 25 individual research projects. By maximizing the number of projects served and minimizing the handling stress for each individual shark, we applied the principles of Reduction and Refinement to study spatial ecology and behavior, reproduction, trophic ecology, environmental health and physiology, population genetics, microbiology and biomedicine, and more aspects of WNA white sharks. Results include a comprehensive understanding of the life history, critical habitats, and threats to YOY, juvenile, subadult, and adult white sharks in the WNA, where the population is currently rebuilding. We next turn our attention and resources to the white shark population of the Eastern North Atlantic (ENA) and Mediterranean Sea, where studies of white sharks have been largely restricted to fisheries records and anecdotal observations, indicating a declining population. In 17 ENA and Mediterranean countries to date, we have established a network of 70 researchers from 55 organizations to collaborate in OCEARCH expeditions in 2023-2025. Focal regions of study will include Scotland, Ireland, England, and France, the western Mediterranean including Malta and Tunisia, and the eastern Mediterranean including the Aegean and Adriatic Seas.

5333: Health assessments in wildlife populations are essential to understanding individual animal, in situ population, and ecosystem health in the face of current and future natural and anthropogenic environmental disturbance. Creating species specific baselines for health comparisons is a critical need across all elasmobranch species. The effectiveness of conservation strategies and scientific sampling protocols that involve handling and live release can be impacted by the animals’ physiological stress response and post-capture mortality. A complete understanding of elasmobranch corticosteroid response to handling, and how changes in blood biochemistry and acid-base analytes relate to this response and predict post-release survival are currently lacking. We report the results of health assessments in white sharks (N=74) sampled as part of a multidisciplinary study in the Western North Atlantic between 2016 and 2022. Physical exam, hematology, plasma chemistry, protein electrophoresis, and acute phase protein responses were evaluated, and preliminary relative reference intervals created along with descriptive statistics. We additionally report the one-alpha hydroxycorticosterone (1aOHB) response to scientific handling of a subset (N=38) of the study animals, using a monoclonal antibody-based enzyme immune assay (EIA). Relationships between all analytes and biologic data (morphometrics, life-history stage [YOY, juvenile, subadult, adult], season, and region) were explored. We further compared 1aOHB values with blood chemistry, acid-base and blood gas alterations traditionally used to monitor stress response. This study creates a baseline for white shark health assessment in the Western North Atlantic, accounting for intrinsic and extrinsic factors, and contributes to a better understanding of their stress response to scientific handling.

These results showed higher δ15N values in Santa Rosalía as a result of baseline differences between the two regions; whereas δ13C values were lower in Bahía Tortugas, suggesting a more oceanic behavior (p<0.05). In Santa Rosalía, there were significant differences by sex in vertebrae for δ15N; whereas δ13C showed ontogenetic shifts, indicating that neonates feed on more coastal areas than juveniles or adults (p<0.05). Neither sex nor ontogenetic differences were observed in Bahía Tortugas (p>0.05), evidencing a high overlap between their isotopic niches. The average trophic level obtained for both tissues was ~ 4, which corresponds to a tertiary predator.
Threatened Species – Spotlight on Mackerel Sharks 3
5335: Global conservation efforts are critical as the world’s ecosystems are under threat from numerous man-made sources. Humans’ behavioral intentions to support conservancy for diverse species and their habitats are predicated on key intrinsic (cognitions, beliefs, affects) and extrinsic factors. One such critical extrinsic factor which is subject to individual differences is former personal experiences with certain animals, such as previous encounters with different species in the wild. This work examined individuals’ self-reported previous experience with two different animal species (sharks and stingrays) to determine their effects on behavioral expressions of tolerance (i.e., willingness to engage in activities in the water at beach facilities that have experienced confirmed sightings of these species within different timeframes). Results inform the design of instructional and promotional materials intended to promote elasmobranch conservation as well as safety materials (e.g., training, signage) that convey information pertaining to risk at beach and oceanic recreation facilities.
5336: Since 2011, the intensity of unprovoked human-shark interaction has dramatically increased on the coast of Reunion Island, with a total of 31 human-shark interactions including 11 fatal shark bites. Most of these interactions occurred within the most popular beaches of the island. The main shark species responsible for these interactions is the bull shark (Carcharhinus leucas). Faced with this unprecedented situation, the French government instituted a ban on all nautical activities around the island and decided to implement a comprehensive strategy to mitigate the risk of human-shark interactions. To ensure the implementation of this strategy, the Reunion Shark Security Centre was officially created in April 2016 and became since June 2020 a French governmental agency. The main objectives of this institution are to coordinate and implement operational mitigation measures contributing to reduce the shark risk in Reunion, as well as to promote mitigation measures reconciling ocean users’ safety and the conservation of marine biodiversity using technological innovations. For the past six years, many innovative mitigation measures have been tested in Reunion waters and other parts of the world. These measures include a highly regulated shark control program using smart drumlines, the creation of new tools to detect potentially dangerous sharks, as well as testing commercially available shark deterrent devices. Thanks to all of these measures, the ban on nautical activities has now been partially lifted in specific areas of the island, with further development to come in the near future.
5337: The whale shark (Rhincodon typus) is an endangered species that seasonally aggregate in the Bay of La Paz, an important feeding ground for juvenile individuals. During the last 20 years, touristic activities involving this species has exponentially increased, growing negative pressure on the animals. Since 2010 The World Wildlife Fund (WWF) in collaboration with the Foundation Telmex Telcel (Alliance WWF-Foundation Telmex Telcel) support the conservation of the whale shark in this region of Mexico. Conservation actions so far implemented include funding local scientists to constantly monitor the presence of the animals and to generate information that is useful in decision-making by the government, encourage education and outreach, support training for guides and captains involved in the touristic activity, habitat improvement through the maintenance of Natural Protected Areas in a post-covid context, and the support to the local authorities in the management of the area of observation. Recently a control center formed by a long distance camara, monitor, and computer was established to guarantee an efficient vigilance of the touristic activity. These actions have achieved a decrease in the shark injuries of 26% since 2016. The collaboration between the civil society organizations such as WWF, private entities, researchers, governs, and local community is essential to achieve the conservation of vulnerable species.

5338: Over the past few years, the number of human-shark interactions have been on the rise globally. A range of measures meant to mitigate the risk of an interaction has been deployed worldwide, such as preventive fishing or exclusion nets. More recently, the use of a personal shark deterrent has become a popular option for ocean users. Several types of these shark deterrents exist and typically rely on optical, olfactive, magnetic, or electrical stimuli to repel sharks that get too close to the wearer. Until recently, these devices were rarely tested independently and in a robust manner. However, this has now changed and through these recent studies, we learned that not all of these devices were effective in repelling sharks, and that electric shark deterrents are generally the most effective type. However, not all of these deterrents are as effective as the others, and their effectiveness may also vary between shark species. Throughout this presentation, we will go over the existing types of personal shark deterrents to identify their advantages and drawbacks, the results of recent investigations on their effectiveness, but also potential future development for this technology.
5339: The International Census of Chondrichthyans in Human Care (aka the ChondroCensus) launched in 2019 at www.sharksandraysproject.com, as part of the framework of the Association of Zoos & Aquariums (AZA) Saving Animals From Extinction (SAFE) Sharks and Rays program. This global census has grown to contain 250 species from 237 facilities across 54 countries world-wide as of May 2022. Besides getting an update count of Chondrichthyans at human care, this platform intends to make this collection of data a truly useful tool for engaging in meaningful, strategic, and collaborative conservation. Stakeholder Teams can complete a survey providing basic husbandry info and add their organizational accrediting body. These data can then be searched by region, organizational accrediting body, genus or species, sex, and the surveyed husbandry criteria. In addition to streamlining periodic reporting required by organizational accrediting bodies, these new features will also anonymously connect stakeholders with each other and with the research community to advance husbandry practices and facilitate collaborative chondrichthyan conservation efforts. Teams always remain anonymous and thus maintain control over their data, as search results are only shown as the number of Teams per ChondroCensus Region. Thus, each stakeholder facility’s Team Coordinator holds the critical role of whether their Team chooses to respond to any requests for connection or information, thereby identifying themselves as stakeholders of the species a search query pertains to.
5340: Australia is a global hotspot of elasmobranch endemicity, making it a global conservation priority to protect the evolutionary diversity of elasmobranchs. Australia is one of 21 regions in the world containing ‘triple threat hotspots’, regions characterised by the presence of threatened species in high levels of richness, endemicity, and evolutionary distinctiveness. The recent ‘Action Plan for Sharks and Rays 2021’ identifies one third (36%) of Australia’s threatened elasmobranch species being endemic. South-eastern quadrant of Australia (southern Queensland through to eastern Victoria) is a region with a high level of incidence of threatened species as a direct result from commercial fishing. Within this region, there are several state-managed fisheries as well as the federally-managed Southern and Eastern Scalefish and Shark Fishery, Australia’s largest by area and volume. To address these issues and support the recovery of threatened endemic species, I will highlight the opportunities that exist in Australian fisheries management, Australia’s environmental laws, and collaborations with NGOs in linking research to policy. The conservation needs for Australian endemic elasmobranchs are urgent, globally recognised, and forecasted to be successful if appropriate actions are implemented.
5341: The short-term socioeconomic impacts of marine spatial conservation measures to the fishing industry, such as the implementation of no-take zones or marine protected areas, often result in these proposals being met with opposition or skepticism, at best. Hence, when spatial conservation measures are implemented to protect a target species or population, they must be strategically located as to maximize their effectiveness, although the field surveys that traditionally underpin this work are time- and resource-intensive. Researchers are therefore increasingly utilizing species distribution models to identify locations of high conservation value. In this study, we aim to establish priority areas for the protection of sharks and rays based on predictions of their distribution in the waters surrounding the Malaysian state of Sabah, in north Borneo. Considering the global decline of elasmobranchs, it is vital for interventions such as spatial conservation management measures to be implemented rapidly and effectively. Here, we use extensive, multi-year bycatch datasets from the Marine Research Foundation for modelling the ranges of species distributions and occurrences of sharks and rays in Sabah. The results of this work will support recommendations for local elasmobranch management measures.
5342: In the last decade, there has been an upsurge in the number of studies that utilise environmental DNA for detecting elasmobranchs, focusing on identifying the presence or absence of species. In this talk, we will explore the application of eDNA methods for long-term and fine-scale monitoring of elasmobranch species. We will present the results from eDNA metabarcoding to assess the diversity of elasmobranchs around a remote atoll in the Chagos Archipelago Marine Protected Area (MPA), showing that eDNA can detect a wide range of elasmobranch species seldom recorded in the MPA. We applied species-specific eDNA methods to assess the distribution of two dominant reef shark species across the archipelago and show that detections were significantly higher around the well-protected atoll of Diego Garcia compared to atolls in the north of the MPA, where detection showed no relationship with concurrent visual surveys or activity hotspots revealed through acoustic telemetry. We infer that populations around the northern atolls have been suppressed by illegal, unregulated and unreported (IUU) fishing activity and that eDNA methods may be limited when investigating species at low population density. In addition, we will showcase how species-specific eDNA methods to investigate the seasonal presence of the Critically Endangered Angelshark (Squatina squatina) and thornback ray (Raja clavata) over the course of a year in Wales. Using both case studies, we emphasise the potential of eDNA methods for elasmobranch monitoring and highlight areas of further research that will be required as they move beyond detection validation into real-world conservation applications.

5343: The movements of stingrays have often been quantified over small localized scales however, it still remains largely unknown whether species display site fidelity or dispersal and to what extent they may connect coastal habitats. This information is vital to inform population dynamics, ecological roles and best management practices for this threatened faunal group. Blue stingrays Dasyatis chrysonota, endemic to southern Africa, are hypothesized to move from shallow inshore habitats to deeper offshore waters during winter, making them a model species to investigate these large-scale movement questions. Twenty-seven individuals were monitored using the Acoustic Tracking Array Platform (ATAP – a nation-wide network of acoustic receivers) for up to 4.5 years. Individuals displayed site fidelity to defined regions of the coast with the majority of detections being recorded in the shallow bay/coastal shelf they were tagged in. However, important movement corridors linking different habitats were identified (inshore vs offshore and coastal bay vs coastal shelf habitats). Modelling highlighted this habitat use was influenced by month and temperature, with individuals displaying restricted movements to the shallow bay habitat in summer when deeper waters were colder. The large collaborative nature of the ATAP allowed for the monitoring of a benthic stingray across large spatial scales (hundreds of kilometres) for the first time, challenging preconceived notions that small undulatory batoids cannot travel large distances (many individuals travelled up to 200 km). Lastly, the current Marine Protected Area zonation may be insufficient to protect blue stingrays from further population declines in South Africa.

5344: The present study was undertaken to assess the diversity, relative abundance and habitat association of elasmobranchs fishes in the nearshore environment on the eastern site of Abu Dhabi, with a focus on how environmental factors impact habitat use and species composition in the shallow lagoons in the world’s hottest sea. Stereo – baited remote underwater video systems (Stereo-BRUVS) in combination with continuous abiotic factor monitoring were used to study elasmobranchs within the area. A great range of environmental changes among the seasons were recorded in salinity and temperature. The video survey recorded two shark species, the blacktip reef shark Carcharhinus melanopterus and the Arabian carpet shark Chiloscyllium arabicum, two shark like rays, halavi guitarfish Glaucostegus halavi and the giant guitarfish Rhynchobatus djiddensis and six ray species, the honeycomb stingray Himantura uarnak, the leopard whipray Himantura leoparda, the pink whipray Pateobatis fai, the cowtail stingray Pastinachus sp., the Arabic whipray Maculabatis arabica and the eagle ray Aetobatus ocellatus. Despite the extreme environmental conditions, the habitat is used by a number of batoids, from which three species are declared critically endangered by the IUCN. This indicates the potential importance of the area in the species life cycle and therefore, the need of conservation management and continuous environmental monitoring in context of a changing climate.

5345: The EMREP project aims to develop technology that integrates electronic reporting (ER) and electronic monitoring (EM) technologies to create an integrated, onboard, monitoring and reporting solution (iEMR) for commercial fishing fleets. As part of the project, the iEMR system is being tested onboard a Portuguese bottom-trawl fishing vessel. It provides a combined tool for the collection of commercial and scientific fishing data, focusing on finding ways to reduce elasmobranch bycatch. The iEMR system makes use of the Olrac fishing eLog system, presently used on hundreds of vessels across fisheries worldwide. The Olrac eLog uses advanced data and communication technologies to facilitate a more accurate, reliable, and efficient approach to the collection, reporting and management of commercial fishing data. Its main advantage is its ability to record data during fishing operations, which can then be used to compile and send out reports needed by a wide range of interested and permitted recipients (commercial, scientific, compliance and management, etc.). The system is also linked to a web-server where data and images from many units across an entire fleet can be stored, analyzed and viewed by different permitted recipients. This iEMR solution provides an innovative and holistic solution to the ever-increasing demand for high quality data within the field of fish resource management. The system is simple to use, allows for data of all kinds (numerical, lookups, free text and images) to be collected and reported and thus transforms every vessel using it into a reliable data collection platform.
